title: The Giant in the Workshop: Florence, 1494–1504
eyes: The Operai of Santa Maria del Fiore (minute books)

Florence, the streets near the Piazza

intro: In November 1494 a French army walked into Florence, the Medici family rode out of it, and a Dominican friar from Ferrara found that the city believed he had foretold it all. Ten years later a seventeen-foot marble nude, carved by a twenty-nine-year-old sculptor from a block that had lain spoiled in the cathedral yard for decades, was hauled through the same streets and set up at the door of the government palace. This chapter lays the eyes of that decade side by side: the years of the friar's republic, its bonfires and its violent end, and the years when the restored republic commissioned the David and set Leonardo and Michelangelo to paint rival battles in its council hall. The backbone is the diary of Luca Landucci, an apothecary whose shop stood at the corner of the Tornaquinci, a few minutes' walk from both the Piazza and San Marco. He wrote short dated notes for half a century: grain prices, executions, sermons, weather, processions. He believed in Savonarola, watched him burn, and six years later noted the hour the marble giant left the cathedral workshop and the night someone threw stones at it. Around him stand voices of very different kinds: the friar's own dated sermons; the memoirs of Philippe de Commynes, the French king's envoy who visited Savonarola in his convent; Michelangelo's letters; Leonardo's dated notes; Machiavelli's letters and the chancery he joined weeks after the execution; a chancery clerk's marginal note in a copy of Cicero; the brother of Botticelli; and the minutes of a committee of artists. Much of this record is not diary in the strict sense. The committee of 25 January 1504 survives as a notarial minute in the archive of the Opera of Santa Maria del Fiore, so it appears here as an institutional eye; the herald Francesco Filarete and the architect Giuliano da Sangallo are known chiefly through what that minute records them saying. Commynes wrote his memoirs after the events. Simone Filipepi's chronicle survives only in extracts. Each eye's form tag says plainly what kind of document it is. The two halves of the decade belong together. The bonfires of 1497 and 1498 burned paintings, mirrors, lutes and books in the same Piazza where the David was later placed, and the republic that the friar's preaching helped found in 1494, with its Great Council and its huge new hall, is the republic that in 1504 wanted a giant at its door and battle scenes on its walls. The committee debated whether the statue should replace Donatello's Judith; the herald argued that Judith, a woman killing a man, had brought the city bad luck. In the end the David took Judith's place on the platform in front of the palace. Savonarola's death on 23 May 1498 is treated here soberly: what Landucci and others wrote, and how the city changed its mind. Where later stories have grown around the David (Vasari's tale of the gonfaloniere and the nose, the claim that Botticelli burned his own paintings), they are flagged as later claims and not presented

title: The Journal and the Poem: Alfoxden and Grasmere, 1797–1803
places: The Quantocks toward Watchet and Lynton
White Moss, between Grasmere and Rydal
Gallow Hill and Brompton church, Yorkshire
intro: In July 1797 William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy took a big, half-furnished house called Alfoxden at the foot of the Quantock Hills in Somerset, three miles from the cottage at Nether Stowey where Samuel Taylor Coleridge lived. For the next year the three of them walked almost daily, by day and by moonlight, and out of those walks came Lyrical Ballads (1798), the book usually taken as the opening of English Romantic poetry. In January 1798 Dorothy began a small journal of weather, light, moon and the people met on the road. After a winter in Germany the Wordsworths settled in December 1799 at a former inn at Town End, Grasmere — the house later called Dove Cottage — and in May 1800 Dorothy began the Grasmere journal, which runs, with a lost notebook for most of 1801, to January 1803. This chapter lays those journals beside the poems that grew from them. Dorothy met an old leech-gatherer on the road in October 1800; William's 'Resolution and Independence' came eighteen months later, and Dorothy copied it out again and again as he revised it. She saw the daffodils by Ullswater on 15 April 1802; 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' was written two years later. She watched London from Westminster Bridge on the morning of 31 July 1802 from the roof of the Dover coach; William's sonnet on the same view was later printed with a wrong date. The journal is not a draft of the poems, and the poems are not copies of the journal: the reader can see where the two lean on each other and where they part. Around the two of them stand other eyes. Coleridge's letters and notebooks run alongside — the November 1797 walk on which the Ancient Mariner was planned, the Keswick years, the verse letter to Sara Hutchinson of 4 April 1802 that became 'Dejection: An Ode'. A Home Office agent, James Walsh, was sent to watch the suspected democrats at Alfoxden in August 1797, and his reports survive. Charles Lamb argued with the poems by post; Robert Southey reviewed the first edition coldly; their Bristol publisher Joseph Cottle and the young William Hazlitt left memoirs of visits to Alfoxden written decades later. John Wordsworth, the sea-captain brother, wrote to Mary Hutchinson about the second edition before his ship was lost in 1805. Annette Vallon, the Frenchwoman who bore William's daughter Caroline in 1792, is present through letters of 1793 that never reached him, and through the August 1802 visit to Calais. Much of the record here is letters and later recollection rather than diary, and the chapter says so entry by entry. Dorothy's journals themselves are not tidy: she often wrote up several days at once and misdated entries, one notebook is lost, and lines in the entry about William's wedding to Mary Hutchinson on 4 October 1802 were later struck through by an unknown hand. Mary and Sara Hutchinson appear mostly through what others wrote to and about them, because few of their own letters from these years survive. The convergences are the shared days: the walk of 1

title: The Ninth: Vienna, 1822–1824
places: Vienna, at Beethoven's side and at the theatre box office
In the audience at the Kärntnertortheater
intro: In November 1822 the Philharmonic Society of London offered Beethoven fifty pounds for a new symphony. He accepted, missed every deadline, and in February 1824 finished a work that ended, unprecedentedly, with soloists and chorus singing Schiller. That same month thirty Viennese patrons, publishers and musicians signed an address begging him not to give the premiere in Berlin. On 7 May 1824 the Ninth Symphony was first played at the court theatre by the Kärntnertor, with the composer on stage, unable to hear it. This chapter is built from conversation books rather than diaries. Beethoven was almost totally deaf; visitors wrote their side of a conversation in pocket notebooks and he answered aloud, so the books preserve half of thousands of exchanges: his nephew Karl counting ticket sales, his secretary Anton Schindler grading the sopranos, Ignaz Schuppanzigh proposing a cheaper hall for the repeat. Around them sit dated letters, published reviews, the London minutes and journal, and a few late recollections. The books are also a crime scene. Schindler, who kept them after Beethoven's death and sold them to Berlin in 1846, added well over a hundred fabricated entries to flatter himself and support his biography. Researchers identified the forgeries in the 1970s and the Berlin edition marks them. Every Schindler entry below states its status, and the most famous image of the night — Caroline Unger turning the deaf composer to see the applause — is given as what it is: a story she told George Grove in 1869, which later scholarship moves from the end of the symphony into the scherzo. The record shows a night that was a triumph in the hall and a let-down at the box office. About 2,200 florins came in and only a few hundred remained. At a dinner two days later Beethoven accused his helpers of cheating him, and the repeat concert on 23 May, at midday in the Redoutensaal, drew a thin house. Within a year the symphony was heard in London in Italian, and in September 1825 the London conductor George Smart came to Baden to meet the composer. Read across, the eyes split along a line of time. Karl, Schindler's genuine entries, Beethoven's own memoranda and the reviewers wrote within hours or days. Holz, Thalberg and Unger wrote or spoke years later, and Schindler's biography and forgeries came later still. The convergences show what each layer adds and what each may have invented.

title: Impression: Paris, 1874
eyes: Société anonyme coopérative des artistes peintres, sculpteurs, graveurs, etc. (charter, catalogue and accounts)
places: Le Havre, a hotel window above the outer harbour
Paris, for Le Sémaphore de Marseille
Cowes and Ryde, Isle of Wight
Argenteuil, with visits to Le Havre and Paris
Studio at 4 rue de Saint-Pétersbourg, Paris
His gallery, rue Laffitte / 11 rue Le Peletier, Paris
intro: On 27 December 1873 a group of painters who were tired of waiting on the Salon jury signed a charter for a joint-stock company: the Société anonyme coopérative des artistes peintres, sculpteurs, graveurs, etc. Monet, Renoir, Sisley, Degas, Morisot and Pissarro were among the first signers. They had no jury and no prizes. Each member paid a subscription, the hanging was settled by lot within groups of similar size, and the society took a commission on sales. Four months later, on 15 April 1874, they opened a month-long show in the empty rooms of the photographer Nadar's former studio at 35 boulevard des Capucines. It ran two weeks ahead of the official Salon, which opened on 1 May at the Palais de l'Industrie. About thirty artists showed some 165 catalogued works. Visitors paid one franc and could come in the evening as well as by day. The best-known pictures now are Monet's harbour at Le Havre, catalogued as 'Impression, soleil levant', Morisot's 'Le Berceau', Renoir's 'La Loge', Cézanne's 'La Maison du pendu' and 'Une moderne Olympia', and Degas's dancers and racecourses. Roughly 3,500 people came, against several hundred thousand at the Salon, and only a handful of works sold. On 25 April Louis Leroy's satire in Le Charivari turned Monet's title into a joke name, 'impressionists'. Four days later Jules Castagnary used the same word seriously in Le Siècle. In December the members voted to wind the company up. This chapter lays those days out through the people who left a dated record of them, and most of that record is letters, published reviews and accounts, not diaries. The painters wrote letters to friends, dealers and family: Pissarro to Théodore Duret, Cézanne to his mother, Morisot to her sister and her mother. Degas wrote to Tissot, and Renoir and Rouart wrote to Caillebotte. The critics wrote in public, on fixed dates. Edmond de Goncourt kept the one true diary here, and he visited Degas's studio two months before the opening. The society's own accounts, its rent, lamp oil, upholstery, police and catalogue sales, survive as a financial statement dated 27 May 1874. Paul Durand-Ruel's memoirs and the painters' late interviews were written decades afterwards. They are flagged as such, because several of the best-known anecdotes, including Monet's story of how 'Impression' got its title, come from them. Seen together, the eyes show how small the event was at the time and how quickly it became a myth. Morisot was the only woman in the show. Her old teacher wrote to her mother that her work had been hung in poisonous company. Her future brother-in-law Manet refused to join and took his chances with the Salon jury. Pissarro had buried his young daughter days before the opening and called the show a success. Cézanne sold a picture to a count and told his mother that he still had to keep working. The chapter follows the year to the Hôtel Drouot auction of 24 March 1875, where the police were called to keep order. It closes with the second group e

title: Vienna 1900: The Secession and the Diaries
places: Berlin; printed in Die Zeit, Vienna
intro: Between the founding of the Secession in April 1897 and the summer of 1914, Vienna produced, in a few square kilometres, new painting, new architecture and design, a new music and a new theory of the mind. The people who made them dined at the same tables, read the same newspapers and attended the same openings. This chapter lays their records side by side: the paintings and the reviews, the concert and the next morning's gossip, the dinner and the diary entry written that night. The honest record is uneven. Arthur Schnitzler kept a near-daily diary for fifty years, and Alma Schindler kept one through her courtships of 1898 to 1902; both were published only in the late twentieth century and are digested here, never quoted. Klimt, the painter at the centre of the storm, left little more than postcards. Most of the other voices are dated letters (Mahler, Freud, Schoenberg), dated newspaper criticism (Hevesi, Bahr) and a satirist's journal (Kraus's Die Fackel). Berta Zuckerkandl, whose salon brought many of them together, wrote her account in exile in 1939 and is marked as memoir. The first great clash came in March 1900, when Klimt's Philosophy, painted for the ceiling of the university, went on show at the Secession. Professors petitioned against it, critics fought for and against it for weeks, and it went on to win a gold medal at the Paris World Exhibition. A few months earlier Freud had published The Interpretation of Dreams to near silence. The two works argued, in different languages, that reason was not the master of the house. The rooms are the heart of the chapter: the Zuckerkandl dinner in November 1901 where Alma Schindler, seated beside her former suitor Klimt, met Mahler; the Beethoven exhibition of April 1902, where painting, sculpture, architecture and Mahler's trombones were meant to make one artwork; the Kunstschau of 1908, where the state bought The Kiss; and the Musikverein on 31 March 1913, where Schoenberg's concert ended in a brawl. Several famous moments survive only as anecdote: Klimt's word on the station platform as Mahler left, Alma's later versions of her marriage, the hostess's memory of the first meeting. They are marked as such. What the contemporary record shows is a city in which a handful of people produced work that was greeted, almost every time, with laughter, petitions and lawsuits, and which they defended by talking, writing and exhibiting together.

title: The Rite of Spring: Paris, 29 May 1913
eyes: Marie Rambert (born Cyvia Rambam; also Miriam Ramberg)
places: Journey from Ustilug to Talashkino, near Smolensk
Monte Carlo, a small rehearsal room
Louis Laloy's house, Bellevue, near Paris
Paris, avenue du Bois de Boulogne
London (company rehearsing at the Aldwych Theatre)
Seat 111 in the stalls, then the wings
A cab to the Bois de Boulogne (by Cocteau's account)
A nursing home at Neuilly, outside Paris
With the company on tour and in rehearsal, winter 1912–13
intro: Le Sacre du printemps began as a picture in two men's heads: a pagan Russian spring in which a girl dances herself to death to placate the earth. The composer Igor Stravinsky and the painter-archaeologist Nicholas Roerich shaped the scenario in 1910–11, finishing it at Princess Tenisheva's craft estate at Talashkino near Smolensk in July 1911. Stravinsky wrote the music in a cramped room at Clarens on Lake Geneva and in Ustilug in Volhynia; he finished the last dance on 17 November 1912. Serge Diaghilev's Ballets Russes gave it to their 23-year-old star Vaslav Nijinsky to choreograph, and the dancers learned it in rehearsal rooms in Berlin, Vienna, Budapest, Leipzig, London and Monte Carlo while the company was on tour. The record of this chapter is mostly not diaries. Some are letters written at the time: Stravinsky to Roerich, to his mother, to Steinberg; Nijinsky to Stravinsky from a Leipzig hotel; Monteux to Stravinsky about horns that could not be heard; Debussy to Stravinsky after playing the score with him. Some are newspaper reviews printed within days of the premiere. One is a true diary entry written that night, by Count Harry Kessler. Much of the most famous testimony, from Stravinsky, Cocteau, Monteux, Rambert, Nijinska and Astruc, was written years or decades later, and it disagrees. Each entry says which kind of source it is. On 29 May 1913 most of these people were in one new building, Gabriel Astruc's Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, opened only eight weeks before. Stravinsky sat in the stalls and then fled backstage; Nijinsky stood on a chair in the wings shouting counts to the dancers; Monteux kept conducting; Rambert was among the dancers who could barely hear the orchestra; Kessler, Cocteau and Roerich watched from the house. Van Vechten, who later said he was there, was probably at the second night. Within forty-eight hours the critics had their say, and Le Figaro's Henri Quittard called the work a laborious and puerile barbarity. Whether that night was a 'riot' remains open. The accounts written at the time describe laughter, whistling, shouted insults and an orchestra drowned out. They also record that the performance ran to the end and that the dancers took curtain calls. The later stories of fights, ejections, police and a challenge to a duel are harder to confirm. Some writers think Diaghilev courted a scandal; others say the hostility came on its own, aimed at the choreography more than the score. This chapter gives each position with its evidence and does not settle it. The chapter ends with two returns. The ballet went to Drury Lane in July 1913 and met a cooler, more puzzled London audience. Then on 5 April 1914 Monteux conducted the music alone at the Casino de Paris, and the audience carried Stravinsky out of the hall on their shoulders. By then Nijinsky had married and been dismissed, his choreography was lost, and within four months Europe was at war.

title: The Bauhaus: Weimar, Dessau, Berlin, 1919–1933
eyes: Thuringian Landtag and Dessau city council (records and press)
places: Weimar 1919–25, Dessau 1925–28, then a private practice in Berlin
Vienna until 1919, Weimar 1919–23, then the Mazdaznan community at Herrliberg near Zurich
Weimar 1922–25, Dessau 1925–31, Berlin, then Black Mountain College, North Carolina, from November 1933
Weimar 1924–25, Dessau 1925–29, then Gropius's Berlin office and industry
intro: In April 1919, five months after the armistice and in the city where a national assembly was drafting Germany's first democratic constitution, the architect Walter Gropius merged two Weimar art schools and called the result the Bauhaus. His manifesto promised to put painters, sculptors and craftsmen back into one workshop and to build a new world together. In fourteen years the school moved twice, had three directors, and outlived three governments that wanted it closed, until its own faculty dissolved it in Berlin in July 1933 rather than accept the conditions of the new regime. This chapter sets the school's people side by side. Oskar Schlemmer's diary and letters are the frankest running commentary on its quarrels. Lyonel Feininger wrote to his wife whenever they were apart, Paul Klee to Lily, and Ise Gropius kept a near-daily chronicle of the director's office from 1924 to 1928. Weavers and metalworkers such as Gunta Stölzl, Anni Albers and Marianne Brandt show the workshops from the bench, where women often began in the jobs the school assigned them and ended up running departments. Much of the honest record here is not diary at all. It is manifestos, circulars, published essays, faculty protocols, and the minutes and votes of the bodies that paid for the school: the Thuringian Landtag in Weimar and the city council of Dessau. These are tagged as what they are. Several diaries, Ise Gropius's among them, are recent publications. Everything is paraphrased, apart from the school's own world-famous slogan of 1923. The convergences fall on the days when these people were in the same rooms: the founding, the exhibition summer of 1923 with its model house and the Triadic Ballet, the masters' self-dissolution at Christmas 1924, the opening of Gropius's glass building in Dessau in December 1926, the handovers of 1928 and 1930, and the last weeks in a disused telephone factory in Berlin-Steglitz. Two kinds of conflict run through the record. Inside the school the masters fought over mysticism and industry, art and social use, and over whether a school could keep out of politics; Hannes Meyer's dismissal in 1930 is reported here as each side described it. Outside it, nationalist and later National Socialist parties attacked the Bauhaus from the first year as foreign, Bolshevist and degenerate, and once in power they closed it. That hostility is set out as the councils, police and Gestapo recorded it.

title: Harlem, 1921–1931
places: Fifth Avenue to Lenox Avenue, Manhattan
New York, then south to Florida and Alabama
Westfield, New Jersey, and New York
Howell's Funeral Home, Seventh Avenue, Harlem
Wilmington, Delaware, and constantly on trains to Philadelphia, Washington and New York
150 West 55th Street, Manhattan, and Harlem's clubs and parties
The Crisis office, 69 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan
Howard University, Washington, D.C., with frequent trips to New York and Europe
The Crisis office, 69 Fifth Avenue, and Harlem
intro: In May 1921 a Black musical opened on West 63rd Street and ran for more than a year; in June The Crisis printed a short poem about rivers by a twenty-year-old named Langston Hughes. Over the next ten years Harlem became the place where Black American writers, artists and musicians made a claim on the nation's culture, and where white New York came to watch, buy and judge. This chapter follows that decade from the inside of its rooms: a club dining room on West 12th Street, a Fifth Avenue restaurant, a townhouse salon on 136th Street, a magazine office downtown, a patron's Park Avenue apartment. Most of the record is letters and dated magazine issues rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. The one true diarist, Alice Dunbar-Nelson, watched from Wilmington, Delaware. Her diary (published in 1984) and her manuscript reading journal log the movement's books, often within days of publication and often on a train, with verdicts of a word or a line. Carl Van Vechten kept daybooks, published in selection in 2003; his entries here rest on his letters and printed introductions. Hughes's own memoir, The Big Sea (1940), is used only where flagged as written later. Because almost all of this material is still in copyright, entries are digests; the few quotations come from magazines printed before 1929. The hinge of the decade was a set of organised occasions. Charles S. Johnson of Opportunity staged the Civic Club dinner of 21 March 1924 and the awards dinner of 1 May 1925. Alain Locke turned the first into the Survey Graphic Harlem number and The New Negro. The young writers answered with Hughes's manifesto in The Nation and the single fiery issue of Fire!! Patronage ran through all of it: Van Vechten's introductions and contacts, Charlotte Mason's secret stipends and contracts, A'Lelia Walker's open house. The record shows each patron as generous and controlling at once, and the protégés saying so themselves. The sharpest argument was over what Black art owed its subjects. When Van Vechten published his Harlem novel in August 1926 under a title many readers found wounding, James Weldon Johnson praised it in Opportunity and Hughes defended it. Du Bois called it a caricature and told readers to drop it in the grate. Two years later he said the same of Claude McKay's Home to Harlem, and McKay answered from Barcelona. These are set out as positions held by people who knew and often admired one another. The historic terms appear only in titles and quotations. The chapter ends with the money gone. The Crash of October 1929 ended much of the white patronage and the downtown visits that had paid for the cabarets and the dinners. Hughes broke with Mason in 1930, his collaboration with Hurston collapsed in Cleveland in February 1931, and A'Lelia Walker died in August. Hughes later chose her funeral as the end of the era, while Dunbar-Nelson's journal for that week lists detective novels.
